solution: \(\sqrt{1+\sin A}=|\sin\tfrac{A}{2}+\cos\tfrac{A}{2}|\). The given equation requires \(\sin\tfrac{A}{2}+\cos\tfrac{A}{2}\le 0\), i.e. \(\sqrt2\,\sin\!\left(\tfrac{A}{2}+\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\le 0\), which holds for \(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\le A\le\tfrac{7\pi}{2}\). Matches option C.
With \(a+b+c=0\), \(x=0\) is one root of the determinant equation; the remaining roots satisfy \(x^2=\tfrac{3}{2}(a^2+b^2+c^2)\), so \(x=\sqrt{\tfrac{3(a^2+b^2+c^2)}{2}}\). Matches option B.

The AP condition \(2\sec\theta=\sec(\theta-\alpha)+\sec(\theta+\alpha)\) reduces to \(\cos^2\theta\,(1-\cos\alpha)=(1-\cos\alpha)(1+\cos\alpha)\). Since \(\cos\alpha\neq1\), \(\cos^2\theta=1+\cos\alpha\), so \(\sin^2\theta=-\cos\alpha\) and \(\sin^2\theta+\cos\alpha=0\). Matches option A.
Scale the second plane by \(\tfrac12\): \(4x-2y+4z+\tfrac{21}{2}=0\). Distance \(=\dfrac{|9-21/2|}{\sqrt{16+4+16}}=\dfrac{3/2}{6}=\dfrac14\). Matches option A.

Circles touching the y-axis at the origin have centre \((a,0)\) and radius \(a\): \(x^2+y^2=2ax\). Differentiating, \(a=x+y\tfrac{dy}{dx}\); substituting back gives \(x^2-y^2+2xy\tfrac{dy}{dx}=0\). Matches option C.
\(\Delta_1=5x-4\) and \(\Delta_2=2x^2+3x\); their sum \(2x^2+8x-4=0\Rightarrow x^2+4x-2=0\Rightarrow x=-2\pm\sqrt6\). Matches option D.
If \(\tfrac{a+b}{2},\,b,\,\tfrac{b+c}{2}\) are in HP then \(\tfrac1b=\tfrac1{a+b}+\tfrac1{b+c}\), which simplifies to \(b^2=ac\). Hence \(a,b,c\) are in GP. Matches option B.
Statement 1 fails at \(n=4\): \(4!/3!=4\), not divisible by 6. Statement 2 fails at \(n=5\): \(5!/3!+3=23\), not divisible by 7. Neither holds, so option D.

\((ZY)X\) is \(3\times3\) (9 entries) — true. \(Y(XZ)\) is \(2\times2\) (4 entries) — true. For \(X(YZ)\): \(YZ\) is \(2\times2\) and \(X\) is \(3\times3\), so the product is undefined — true. All three correct, option D.
Here \(T_k=\binom{n}{k}\), so the expression is \(1+\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^k k\binom{n}{k}\). Since \(\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k k\binom{n}{k}=0\) for \(n\ge2\), the value is \(1+0=1\). Matches option D.

By Fermat's theorem \(f'(0)=0\) (statement A is true). \(f''(0)<0\) is sufficient but not necessary for a local maximum — e.g. \(f(x)=-x^4\) has \(f''(0)=0\) yet a local max at 0 — so statement B need not hold. Only A is correct, option A.

Let \(p^x=q^y=r^z=k\), so \(\ln p=\tfrac{\ln k}{x}\), \(\ln q=\tfrac{\ln k}{y}\), \(\ln r=\tfrac{\ln k}{z}\). Statement II: \((\ln q)^2=(\ln p)(\ln r)\iff y^2=xz\), true since \(x,y,z\) are in GP. Statement I (\(p,q,r\) in AP) fails in general. Only II is correct, option B.
Let \(\alpha=\cot^{-1}3\), so \(\cot2\alpha=\tfrac{4}{3}\). Then \(\cot\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{4}-2\alpha\right)=7\), so \(\cot^2=49\) and \(\sqrt{15+49}=\sqrt{64}=8\). Matches option C.

text: Let \(f(x)=|x|+1\), \(g(x)=[x]-1\), \(h(x)=\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}\), where \([\cdot]\) is the greatest integer function. What is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^-}h(x)+\lim_{x\to0^+}h(x)\) equal to?
solution: As \(x\to0^-\): \(f\to1\), \(g=[x]-1=-2\), so \(h\to-\tfrac12\). As \(x\to0^+\): \(f\to1\), \(g=-1\), so \(h\to-1\). Sum \(=-\tfrac32\). Matches option A.

text: If \(\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3+i & -1 \\ 3-i & 0 & i-1 \\ -1 & -1-i & 1 \end{vmatrix} = A + iB\) where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\), then what is \(A+B\) equal to?
solution: Expanding the Hermitian determinant gives \(-6+0i\), so \(A=-6\), \(B=0\) and \(A+B=-6\). Matches option B.
